article.title: Upsurges Bubble Around the Globe but Will it Evolve into Effective Change?
article.author: Michael Albert
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Reports show activism of many minds, addressing many topics and reaching considerable scale erupting in many places. Education, housing, corruption, jobs, prices, immigration, regimentation, fascism, war, data centers, weather, electoral campaigns, and more. France, Spain, Belgium, Albania, Brazil, Serbia, India, Nepal, Bangladesh, and more. What to do? On the one hand, where you are, if it arrives, participate. If it hasn’t yet arrived, try to initiate it. So far, so obvious. But a larger, overarching possibility beckons. Spread the eruption. Enlarge each outbreak. Make it all last. Still obvious. But how? What can turn a temporary eruption that may or may not win some specific immediately focused local aims into a sustained wave of activism that grows, persists and finally wins not only various initially sought aims, but whole new societies in a revolutionized world? Isn’t that the strategic question we must now address? Related: Rethinking Working-Class Resistance: Flipping the Script Without persistence we win some gains, but not many. We go a ways, but not far. To achieve more we must expand our efforts from upsurge to persistence. From single issue to multi issue. From public policy to systemic structure. And from shocking on-lookers to rousing and welcoming them. Upsurge alone may win some gains but it will not reach the causal core of society’s problems or potentials. To upsurge is not bad. Upsurges spread activism. To address a pressing issue is not bad. To address pressing issues inspires involvement and grows commitment. To overturn horrible public policy is not bad. To overturn public policies alleviates pain and teaches tactics. All of that counters passivity and fuels momentary hope. But significant victory requires sustained participation. To overturn the causes of contemporary suffering and attain preferred positive alternatives requires contagious persistent commitment. But how can we exceed our moment’s justified passions? How can initial narrowness reach out broadly? How can narrow focus diversify greatly? How can limited commitment deepen humanely? How can we develop sufficient coherence to confront and overturn existing institutions? How can we seek and finally implement a just, liberatory, self-managed future? For French high school students to demand equitable education is excellent. When they and their teachers and wider circles of workers and unions demand books not bombs, and then affordability for all, it makes critical connections that take resistance another step forward. When Spaniards add to demanding affordable housing, demanding quality education, it also takes a step forward. And when masses of neighborhood resisters add to ending corruption their desires to attain participatory democracy, or when union resisters add to preserving jobs desires to establish self-managed workers councils, or when consumer resisters add to attaining affordability desires to conceive and ultimately implement participatory planning, or when citizen resisters add to blocking fascism desires to enlarge participation, or everyone adds to ending war desires to wage peace, or adds to stopping data centers desires to develop people centers, or adds to ending fossil fuels desires to establish environmental justice, or adds to electoral campaigning desires to reconstruct governance, all that takes essential steps forward. But beyond diversifying, what can sustain upsurge? How does to briefly seek single issue public policy gains become to persistently seek multi-issue systemic institutional gains? If we don’t explore how movement enrichment can come about, how will we sensibly bring it about? Strategy can’t usefully be an afterthought of the decision to leave school, leave work, or leave home to go wild in the streets. Strategy has to propose flexible agendas—what to demand, what to close down, what to assemble. It has to conceive agendas for us to continually refine, correct, and implement in light of lessons we cull from experience. Whatever attracts more support, more participants, we do that. Whatever doesn’t. We reject that. Okay, but what features must a sustained multi-issue movement have that a single or even multi-issue upsurge needs to attain? How can those who desire fundamental change contribute to attaining those needed features? Persistent movements have participants who become driven by more than provocative slogans and desires. By more than anger and energy. Persistent movements have members whose wants grow beyond their initial passions. The mood and even the psychology of persistent movements’ members alters from short-term immediate spontaneous demonstrations to long-term carefully pursued plans. Activists’ moods rise beyond living to earn or living to survive, to living to win. Moods becomes confident but also careful, militant but also welcoming. Movements become alert to their implications. Indeed, persistent movements continuously calculate consequences. They pursue what will enlarge their numbers, deepen their commitment, and enrich their aims. They combine outreach with lasting organizational structure. They reject actions, words, or deeds that repel constituencies they need to attract. They pursue what will abet winning and reject what will obstruct winning. Upsurges happen when something that typically differs each time it appears—sometimes it may be masses volunteering, other times it may be masses rioting—ignites angry pain many others feel into positive demands for real gains. When something in whatever shape it emerges turns resigned acceptance of horrid, grim conditions to reasoned hope that strategic actions can and will yield better conditions. But to become sustained, strategic, and revolutionary requires more than a surge. Upsurge is in the air, more here, less there, to be sure—but if you look, you can see it happening or ready to happen there and here too, and maybe even all over. Will upsurge grow into sustained, collective, strategic commitment that persists until it achieves fundamental change? Upsurge is exciting. Upsurge is even wonderful. But its final grade depends on its consequences. I am 79. I was lucky to have participated in an earlier upsurge called the Sixties. It was heroic. It was solidaritous. It was passionate. It even spanned years. It won a lot but not fundamental change. We were insufficiently visionary for that. We were insufficiently strategic for that. We tried, but in the end, we did not win that. Ours was of course not the first upsurge that fell short or got waylaid. And there were more, too, between then and now. We lose, we lose, we lose, but when we learn sufficiently, we will win. I have always abhorred apocalyptic politics. But the simple fact is, the time has come to learn, to organize, and to fight until we win another world that is possible. And here, where I live perhaps close your eyes, open your mind, and listen to Leonard Cohen: It’s coming to America first, the cradle of the best and of the worst. It’s here they got the range It’s here they got the range and the machinery for change and it’s here they got the spiritual thirst. It’s here the family’s broken and it’s here the lonely say that the heart has got to open in a fundamental way: Democracy is coming to the U.S.A. Or if you prefer, listen to young Bobby: Oh, the foes will rise With the sleep still in their eyes And they’ll jerk from their beds and think they’re dreamin’ But they’ll pinch themselves and squeal And know that it’s for real The hour when the ship comes in Then they’ll raise their hands Sayin’ we’ll meet all your demands But we’ll shout from the bow your days are numbered And like Pharaoh’s tribe They’ll be drownded in the tide And like Goliath, they’ll be conquered This article was produced by Z Network .
